Genomes encoded genes associated with efflux, target modification, motility/adhesion, and stress adaptation, indicating environmental resilience rather than clinical pathogenicity. Overall, these isolates displayed limited pathogenic phenotypes with genomic traits primarily supporting environmental adaptation and survival.

title: Escherichia coli bacteriophage vB_EcoS_MS2 effectively prevents biofilm formation but shows limited activity against mature biofilms
abstract: Pathogenic Escherichia coli biofilms pose a significant challenge in veterinary and clinical settings due to their high antibiotic resistance. This study characterizes the E. coli bacteriophage vB_EcoS_MS2 as a potential targeted biocontrol agent against these pathogens. Host range determination revealed high specificity, with vB_EcoS_MS2 lysing only select E. coli strains and demonstrating superior replication efficiency (Efficiency of Plating: 112.57%) on strain C4 compared to its propagation host, MS2. While nutrient limitation strongly induced biofilm formation in in vitro assays, phage vB_EcoS_MS2 demonstrated potent prophylactic activity, inhibiting initial biofilm development by over 70% across all tested concentrations (10⁴-10⁹ PFU/mL). Conversely, the phage showed limited and transient efficacy in eradicating mature, 48-hour-old biofilms under the tested conditions. Whole-genome sequencing confirmed a 40,209 bp circular genome belonging to the class Caudoviricetes, encoding a robust holin-endopeptidase lytic cassette without carrying known antimicrobial resistance determinants. These findings indicate that while vB_EcoS_MS2 is highly effective for prophylactic biofilm prevention, complementary strategies may be required to clear established biofilms.

title: The structural context of mutations in proteins predicts their effect on antibiotic resistance
abstract: In, a prevalent and deadly pathogen, resistance to antibiotics evolves primarily through non-synonymous mutations in proteins. Sequence-based analyses can uncover the genetic basis of antibiotic resistance, but these methods focus on primary sequence and often neglect other biological signals, such as protein structural information. We hypothesize that integrating the structural context of mutations improves the prediction of effects on function and phenotype. We curate high-confidence structural annotations for theproteome from 1350 crystallography and 2337 AlphaFold predictions, and mutations from over 31,000isolates. We demonstrate that mutations in proteins known to cause resistance are clustered in 3D space, even in proteins where inactivating mutations at any position are thought to cause resistance. We find over 450 proteins in theproteome that display signals of clustered mutations, many of which have a known relationship with antibiotic resistance. We show that a supervised classifier trained on 3D distance to known resistance sites alone has an1 score of 96.5% at classifying mutations as resistance-conferring on a held-out test set. This work demonstrates that protein structure provides useful information for categorizing which variants may cause antibiotic resistance, even when the majority of structures are AI-predicted.

title: The dual action of Mume Fructus against Helicobacter pylori: targeting bacterial viability and virulence
abstract: To tackle the global challenge ofantibiotic resistance, this study screened aqueous extracts from 17 edible plants with reported anti-potential and found Mume Fructus extract (MFE) as a potential food-derived anti-candidate, and subsequently investigated its efficacy and mechanisms. MFE exerted potent and consistent inhibitory activity against both standard and multidrug-resistant (MDR)strains. It alleviated gastric inflammation and restored the mucosal structure in mice, and protected GES-1 cells from-induced damage in a dose-dependent manner. Organic acids were identified as the potential key compounds with enhanced cytoprotective effects. MFE and its organic acids significantly downregulatedvirulence genes, whereas organic acids bound to the CagA oncoprotein. These findings suggest that MFE exerts anti-effects through direct bacterial growth suppression and virulence attenuation. Given its potent anti-MDR strain activity and favorable safety, MFE represents a promising functional food ingredient for the adjunctive dietary management ofinfection.

title: Hospital wastewater-based antimicrobial resistance epidemiology: a scoping review
abstract: Wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE) offers pooled biological samples of defined populations, complementing clinical surveillance for infectious diseases. Hospitals are hotspots for antimicrobial resistance (AMR). We performed a scoping review assessing hospital wastewater for AMR monitoring. We searched Medline, Embase, Biosis, Web of Science, and biorxiv.org from inception to May 5, 2026, for studies using hospital wastewater to monitor AMR. The primary outcome was AMR detection and concordance with traditional surveillance. Concordance was reported by resistance class, and reported as strain- or gene-level, as discordant, or as not assessed. Secondary outcomes included sampling methods, and laboratory techniques. Of 4,695 screened studies, 36 from 22 countries met inclusion criteria (high-income 53%, upper-middle-income 42%, and lower-middle-income 5%). Traditional surveillance used mostly routine diagnostics (58%); only 39% of studies aligned temporally with wastewater sampling. Extended-Spectrum Beta-Lactamase-producing organisms showed strain-level concordance in 2/6 studies, and gene-level concordance in 4/6; carbapenem resistance showed strain-level concordance in 2/9 and gene-level concordance in 4/9. Concordance was present for vancomycin-resistant enterococci (2/3), while inconsistent for(0/2) and. One study quantified correlation statistically, finding strong association (Spearman's rho = .88). Wastewater sampling methods included grab sampling (39%), composite sampling (36%), and was unreported (25%). Most studies combined culture-based (89%) and molecular methods (PCR 75%, WGS 42%, metagenomics 17%), mostly targeting Gram-negatives (83%). Hospital WBE showed variable concordance with traditional surveillance, but methodological heterogeneity and limited temporal alignment constrain comparisons. Standardized frameworks and patient-level studies, particularly from low- and middle-income countries, are needed.

title: Biodegradation Characteristics of Piperacillin by Marine Bacillus cereus PP1 and Genome-Guided Mining of Candidate β-Lactamases
abstract: Antibiotic residues in aquatic environments are an increasing concern because they may retain antibacterial activity, promote antibiotic resistance and generate transformation products with uncertain ecological risks. In this study, marine-derived bacteria were screened for their ability to degrade representative β-lactam antibiotics. Strain PP1, identified as Bacillus cereus, was selected for detailed characterization because of its outstanding degradation capacity toward piperacillin, ceftiofur and cephalexin, especially its efficient removal of piperacillin at a high initial concentration of 100 mg/L. During a 48-h incubation, B. cereus PP1 completely degraded piperacillin and reduced the antibacterial activity of the treated solution against representative Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria. UHPLC-MS/MS analysis indicated that piperacillin was transformed mainly through β-lactam ring opening, together with side-chain cleavage and downstream fragmentation reactions. The degradation products showed no obvious hemolytic activity under the tested conditions, whereas live PP1 exhibited hemolysis, highlighting the need for biosafety evaluation before live-cell application. Whole-genome sequencing revealed that PP1 contains a single circular chromosome of 5,285,738 bp and has broad metabolic potential. CARD, CAZy and VFDB annotations indicated antibiotic tolerance, hydrolytic enzyme resources and virulence-associated features. Targeted mining using a local β-lactamase database identified two candidate β-lactamase genes, PP1_BLA_A and PP1_BLA_B, assigned to class A and class B β-lactamases, respectively. Structure prediction and molecular docking further suggested that both enzymes can accommodate piperacillin, but with distinct binding modes. These findings indicate that B. cereus PP1 is a valuable source for β-lactamase discovery and enzyme-based β-lactam bioremediation.

title: Whole-genome insights into a multidrug-resistant, biofilm-forming, and pathogenic Salmonella Umbilo isolate and molecular characterization of rare Salmonella serovars from poultry
abstract: Salmonellosis is one of the leading foodborne zoonoses worldwide, with contaminated poultry products representing a major source of human infection. This study characterized rare Salmonella serovars circulating in poultry flocks with respect to biofilm formation, virulence, antimicrobial resistance (AMR), CRISPR loci diversity, and genomic features. Salmonella isolates were conventionally isolated from drug swap samples and serotyped. Biofilm- (csgA, csgB, csgD, ompR, adrA, rpoS, and fimH) and virulence-associated genes (sipA, sipD, sopB, sopD, sopE, sopE2, sitC, sifA, ssaR, spvC, and pefA) were investigated. CRISPR loci and phenotypic AMR were examined. The Salmonella isolate, which exhibited the highest MAR index, was analyzed by whole-genome sequencing (WGS). Bioinformatic analyses were conducted to determine its plasmid, AMR, and virulence capacity. Thirty rare Salmonella serovars were identified including, Aba, Atento, Ball, Blegdam, Bonariensis, Bradford, Chandans, Fallowfield, Ferruch, Idikan, II (1,9,12:g,m,s,t:e,n,x), Inganda, Korbol, Leeuwarden, Menden, Naestved, Ohlstedt, Papuana, Petahtikve, Sandow, Schwarzengrund, Svedvi, Telaviv, Thompson, Tinda, Tsevie, Tumodi, Umbilo, Uppsala, and Vejle. CsgA-B-C (100.0%) and sipA (96.7%) were the most prevalent genes. S. Sandow harbored all examined genes. CRISPR2 locus (23.3%) was more prevalent than the CRISPR1 locus (3.3%). Resistance to streptomycin (56.7%) and sulfonamides (46.7%) was most common, whereas 40.0% of the isolates were MDR. WGS of the S. Umbilo isolate, which exhibited the highest MAR index (0.48), identified the IncHI2A plasmid (a key factor in horizontal transfer of AMR genes), 12 AMR genes (responsible for resistance to beta-lactams, aminoglycosides, phenicols, and lincosamides), and 181 virulence-associated genes (involved in adhesion, invasion, chemotaxis, intracellular survival, and environmental persistence). The detection of highly resistant and potentially pathogenic S. Umbilo, previously linked to a multinational foodborne outbreak in Europe, highlights its potential public health significance. MLST further proved useful for serovar prediction, with ST2014. Rare Salmonella serovars circulating in poultry flocks possess substantial virulence, biofilm-forming, and AMR potential. These findings highlight the importance of including rare serovars in surveillance and control programs to mitigate foodborne transmission and the spread of AMR.

title: Genomic insights into high-sugar tolerance and probiotic properties of Pediococcus pentosaceus MP13, a potential probiotic isolated from traditional fermented rose jam
abstract: Pediococcus pentosaceus MP13 was previously isolated from traditionally fermented rose jam, a high-sugar fermentation environment. This strain exhibits promising fermentation and probiotic-related properties, but the genomic features potentially associated with its tolerance to high-sugar conditions remain unclear. This study evaluated the effects of sugar stress, selected probiotic properties, and characterized genomic features of MP13. Increasing sugar concentrations inhibited MP13 growth and increased extracellular conductivity and nucleic acid leakage, both approaching plateaus at higher concentrations, while cells exposed to 55% sugar retained relatively intact coccoid morphology. MP13 also showed appreciable cell surface hydrophobicity, approximately 75% auto-aggregation, and inhibitory activity against the tested indicator bacteria. Its complete genome comprised a single 1 939 576 bp circular chromosome with a GC content of 38.46%. Comparative genomic analysis showed high overall similarity to related P. pentosaceus strains, while revealing inter-strain genomic variation. MP13 utilized 22 of 49 tested carbohydrates, and genome annotation identified diverse carbohydrate metabolism-related pathways, 212 putative CAZyme genes, and 33 substrate-specific PTS genes, suggesting broad genetic potential for carbohydrate metabolism despite phenotype-genotype discrepancies for sucrose and d-melibiose. Functional annotation identified genes with predicted roles in osmotic, acid, and bile stress responses, and adhesion, while genome mining revealed putative bacteriocin-associated loci. Safety assessment showed a non-hemolytic phenotype and no known toxin or biogenic amine biosynthesis genes, while no corresponding known acquired antimicrobial resistance genes determinants were detected for previously reported resistance to gentamicin, erythromycin, and penicillin. The phenotypic and genomic characteristics of P. pentosaceus MP13 support its further evaluation for sugar-rich food fermentation and as a probiotic candidate. Carbohydrate metabolism- and stress-response-related genomic features suggest potential contributions to high-sugar tolerance, but their functional roles require expression- and function-based validation. © 2026 Society of Chemical Industry.

title: [Translated article] The "Trojan horse" against antimicrobial resistance: Siderophore conjugates and public health
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance, particularly in carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales such as KPC-type, represents a critical threat to public health in Latin America, associated with high mortality rates and increased healthcare costs. This systematic review aims to evaluate the therapeutic potential of siderophore-drug and siderophore-peptide conjugates against priority multidrug-resistant pathogens, including Enterobacterales, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Acinetobacter baumannii, analyzing their efficacy, mechanisms of action, and implementation challenges. A systematic search was conducted in the PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science databases up to August 2025. Key terms such as "siderophore conjugates", "Trojan horse antibiotics", "antimicrobial resistance", and "Gram-negative bacteria" were used. Preclinical and clinical studies, reviews, and meta-analyses published between 2019 and 2025 were included, selecting 55 references based on relevance to the topic, currency, and methodological quality. This review is a narrative review with a systematic literature search, developed in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. Siderophore conjugates, via the "Trojan horse" mechanism, effectively exploit bacterial iron uptake systems to deliver antimicrobial agents in a targeted manner. They overcome key resistance mechanisms such as β-lactamase production, porin alterations, and efflux pump activity, while reducing systemic toxicity and preserving commensal microbiota. Clinical evidence (e.g., cefiderocol) and preclinical studies confirm their efficacy against multidrug-resistant (MDR) and extensively drug-resistant (XDR) strains, achieving significant reductions in minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs). However, critical challenges were identified: optimization of chemical stability and intracellular drug release, complexity in synthesis and industrial scaling under Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) standards, and regulatory and logistical barriers in resource-limited settings. Siderophore conjugates offer a targeted therapeutic approach against multidrug-resistant pathogens by exploiting the bacteria's own iron-uptake systems. The available evidence ranges from clinical results with cefiderocol to preclinical developments with other platforms. Their application, however, faces challenges that span chemical optimization, manufacturing, regulation, and access in clinical settings.

title: Neisseria gonorrhoeae antimicrobial resistance trends in Portugal over four decades, 1983-2025
Antimicrobial resistance in invasive infections among patients with cirrhosis in Latin America: A multicenter registry
Combating Antimicrobial Resistance: Emerging Non-Traditional Therapeutics, Clinical Translation Challenges, and Future Perspectives
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) has emerged as one of the most severe global health threats. The rapid expansion of multidrug-resistant (MDR) and extensively drug-resistant (XDR) pathogens compromises the effectiveness of conventional antibiotics. Globally, ESKAPE organisms (Enterococcus faecium, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Enterobacter spp.) have led to therapeutic failure, prolonged hospitalization, and increased mortality rates. This review identifies the molecular mechanisms, including enzymatic antibiotic inactivation, efflux pump overexpression, biofilm formation, and horizontal gene transfer, that underline the resistance of disseminated pathogens to antibiotics in clinical, agricultural, and environmental settings. Antibiotic overuse and pharmaceutical and agricultural discharges create persistent reservoirs for the dissemination of AMR genes. Furthermore, we evaluated the non-traditional antibacterial efficacy of antimicrobial peptides, bacteriophage therapy, monoclonal antibodies, probiotics, fecal microbiota transplantation, anti-virulence agents, CRISPR-Cas precision antimicrobials, and nanotechnology-based drug delivery platforms. Current preclinical and clinical evidence indicates the eradication of resistant pathogens, disruption of biofilms, and preservation of host microbiota, thereby reducing the selective pressure associated with broad-spectrum antibiotics. Despite these advances, major translational barriers, such as pharmacokinetic instability, manufacturing limitations, and insufficient clinical validation, restrict the implementation of the framework. In the future, the AMR management framework will require precision medicine, artificial intelligence, and One Health-based integration via multidisciplinary collaboration.

title: Dynamics of emm types in invasive Streptococcus pyogenes isolates from Argentina, 2018-2024
abstract: Group A Streptococcus (GAS) is a major cause of invasive bacterial infections worldwide, making molecular surveillance essential for monitoring strain dynamics and detecting emerging lineages. We conducted nationwide molecular surveillance of invasive GAS (iGAS) infections in Argentina between July 2018 and December 2024, analyzing 1127 isolates from confirmed cases. emm typing was performed using Sanger sequencing (2018-2020) and whole-genome sequencing (WGS) (2022-2024), enabling multilocus sequence typing (MLST), virulence and antimicrobial resistance profiling. Surveillance was interrupted during 2020-2021 due to the COVID-19 pandemic but was strengthened thereafter when iGAS became nationally notifiable. Overall, 59 emm types and 61 sequence types were identified. emm1 predominated across the study period (42.4%), followed by emm12, emm3, and emm4, with marked temporal shifts. In 2023, clonal diversity declined, with emm1 and emm12 accounting for 72% of isolates and the emergence of hypervirulent M1 lineages. In 2024, emm diversity increased, with expansion of emm3, emm4, emm49, and emm87.

title: Nurse-Led and Nurse-Involved Antimicrobial Stewardship in Hospitals and Primary Care: Protocol for a Mixed Methods Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis With Gulf Cooperation Council and Middle East and North Africa Subgroup Analysis
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance poses a growing threat to patient safety worldwide. Nurses are central to antimicrobial management; however, their contribution to formal antimicrobial stewardship (AMS) programs remains poorly characterized. To our knowledge, no previous review has combined evidence on the effectiveness and implementation of nurse-led and nurse-involved AMS interventions, including Gulf Cooperation Council and Middle East and North Africa (GCC/MENA) subgroup analysis. This protocol describes a mixed methods systematic review that aims to determine (1) the effectiveness of nurse-led or nurse-involved AMS interventions on patient and antimicrobial outcomes in hospital and primary care settings and (2) the barriers and facilitators influencing this implementation using the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR 2.0). This review follows the Joanna Briggs Institute convergent, parallel-streams mixed methods methodology. Eligible studies report a nurse-led or nurse-involved AMS intervention among adults receiving antimicrobial therapy in hospital or primary care settings; pediatric-only and long-term care settings are excluded. Eleven databases will be searched from January 2000 to the calendar month of searching. Two reviewers will independently screen records in 2 rounds, with agreement quantified by Cohen κ (target ≥0.70). The quantitative stream will include randomized, quasi-experimental, interrupted time series, and controlled before-and-after studies, with effect measures matched to outcome type. Risk of bias will be independently assessed using design-matched tools. Random-effects meta-analysis will be the primary approach, with prediction intervals supplementing² to quantify heterogeneity. The qualitative stream will synthesize implementation data through hybrid deductive-inductive CFIR 2.0 thematic synthesis. Both streams will be integrated through a convergent joint display classifying findings as convergent, complementary, expansive, or discordant. Three primary subgroup analyses will compare GCC/MENA vs the rest of the world, hospital vs primary care, and levels of nursing involvement. GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation) will be applied to all primary quantitative outcomes. Database searches, Covidence import, and deduplication were completed in March 2026. Title and abstract screening, including pilot calibration, was completed by June 2026. Full-text screening was planned for completion by August 2026, followed by parallel quantitative and qualitative data extraction from August to September 2026. Meta-analysis, CFIR thematic synthesis, and GRADE assessment are expected by November 2026, with mixed methods integration planned for November to December 2026. Manuscript writing is planned for January to February 2027, with submission targeted for March 2027. No amendments to the registered protocol have occurred. This review is intended to provide one of the first meta-analytic syntheses of nurse-led and nurse-involved AMS clinical effectiveness alongside a structured implementation analysis. Findings may inform stewardship program design, nursing education, and health policy, particularly in GCC/MENA settings where nursing AMS evidence is scarce.

title: A Dual-Amplification DNA Fluorescence Biosensor Based on Strand Displacement
abstract: The development of high-sensitivity biosensing architectures with integrated signal processing capabilities remains a cornerstone of molecular diagnostics. To address the requirements for ultralow-concentration detection, we developed a programmable and modular dual-amplification DNA fluorescent biosensor (DDFB). This platform features a decoupled architecture that synergistically integrates an upstream entropy-driven catalytic (EDC) circuit for initial signal gain with a downstream hybridization chain reaction (HCR) for high-order reporting. As an enzymefree logic-capable system, the DDFB exhibited an experimentally supported linear range of 100 pM-10 nM for ARG detection, spanning two orders of magnitude, with an estimated LOD of 9.14 pM calculated using the 3σ/S criterion. Furthermore, this detection scheme enables versatile platform expansion through modular design, which exhibits superior performance in the detection of both antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) and miR-141. Collectively, this research provides a robust, reconfigurable framework for next-generation nanobiosensors and information-processing DNA circuits.

title: Genome-wide synthetic lethality screen of Bam complex-associated genes in Escherichia coli
abstract: Biogenesis of the bacterial outer membrane is key to bacterial survival and antibiotic resistance. Central to this is the β-barrel assembly machine (Bam) complex and its associated chaperones, which are responsible for transport, folding, and insertion of outer membrane proteins (OMPs). TheBam complex is composed of two essential subunits, BamA and BamD, and three non-essential accessory lipoproteins, BamB, BamC, and BamE. Optimal Bam function is further dependent on the non-essential periplasmic chaperones DegP, Skp, and SurA. Despite intensive study, the specific function of these non-essential Bam-associated proteins is not fully understood. Here, we analysed Δ, Δ, Δ, Δ, Δand Δknockout strains by phenotypic screening, conservation analysis and high-throughput genetics. We identified hundreds of synthetic-lethal interactions and revealed that Bam complex activity is impacted by changes in outer membrane lipid composition and that enterobacterial common antigen is essential in the absence of the chaperone SurA. We also show that genes responsible for synthesis of peptidoglycan are synthetically lethal with Bam accessory lipoprotein encoding genes. Together, our data indicate potential mechanisms for coordination of OMP biogenesis with other cellular growth processes, such as LPS and peptidoglycan biogenesis.

title: Phenotypic and genotypic assessment of antimicrobial and biocide resistance in enterobacteria from anaerobic digestion of dairy waste: implications for environmental and public health
abstract: Antimicrobial-resistant bacteria in agricultural waste represent a critical One Health concern. Anaerobic digestion of livestock waste is widely promoted; however, the fate of antimicrobial resistance and biocide tolerance in full-scale systems remains unclear, constraining safe digestate reuse. This study assessed phenotypic and genotypic resistance in Escherichia coli-like enterobacteria isolated from effluent and biofertilizer in a full-scale dairy anaerobic digestion system. A total of 173 isolates were screened for antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs), antimicrobial susceptibility, multidrug resistance (MDR), and biocide inhibition-zone responses. No diarrheagenic virulence genes were detected. At least one screened ARG was detected in 91.0% of effluent and 83.3% of biofertilizer isolates. qacE∆1 was the most frequent marker and occurred significantly more often in effluent (70.8%) than biofertilizer isolates (44.0%; q = 0.00291). Phenotypic resistance to at least one antimicrobial was observed in 27.0% and 34.5% of effluent and biofertilizer isolates, respectively, while MDR occurred in 2.2% and 9.5% (p = 0.0521). tet(a) carriage was strongly associated with tetracycline resistance (OR = 20.9; q < 0.001). HOinhibition zones were significantly smaller among biofertilizer isolates, whereas Lactic Acid (LA) yielded 6-mm measurements in all isolates and in the reference strain. These findings demonstrate that anaerobic digestion does not fully eliminate culturable resistant enterobacteria and underscore the need for integrated resistance monitoring in dairy-waste management.

title: Natural Product-Based Strategies for Combating Antimicrobial Resistance in ESKAPE Pathogens
abstract: The increase of antimicrobial resistance (AMR), particularly among the ESKAPE pathogens (Enterococcus faecium, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Enterobacter spp. poses a critical global threat to public health by severely limiting effective therapeutic options. These pathogens employ diverse and efficient survival strategies, including drug-degrading enzymes, target modification, porin loss, efflux pump overexpression, and biofilm formation, leading to multidrug-resistant (MDR), extensively drug-resistant (XDR), and pan-resistant clinical phenotypes. As conventional antibiotic discovery slows and treatment failures rise, natural products have re-emerged as a promising source of chemically diverse leads with antibacterial activity. Plants and microbes biosynthesize structurally diverse secondary metabolites such as polyketides, alkaloids, flavonoids, phenolics, terpenoids, and saponins, many of which exhibit broad-spectrum antibacterial activity and synergize with existing antibiotics while exerting reduced selective pressure for resistance. Several compounds demonstrated potent antibacterial activity with MIC values ranging from 0.1 to 32 µg/mL, highlighting their therapeutic potential. This review provides a comprehensive analysis of natural product-based strategies against ESKAPE pathogens, highlighting their mechanisms of action: membrane disruption, inhibition of efflux pumps, interference with DNA/protein synthesis, suppression of quorum sensing, and inhibition of biofilm formation. Special emphasis is placed on alkaloids, flavonoids, and terpenoids whose antibacterial potential is closely linked to defined structure-activity relationships (SAR). Alkaloids such as berberine, sanguinarine, and conessine show potent activity by targeting cell wall integrity, FtsZ-mediated division, and efflux systems, while specific flavonoid subclasses exhibited enhanced antibacterial potency through key structural features such as 5,7-dihydroxylation, prenylation, and optimized B-ring substitutions. Numerous natural products discussed demonstrate clinically relevant activity against MDR S. aureus, carbapenem-resistant K. pneumoniae, A. baumannii, and P. aeruginosa, supporting their potential as lead compounds or adjuvant agents.

title: Molecular Characterization of vanA and bla(TEM) Mutant Genes in Enterococcus faecalis: In silico and in vitro investigation of Sitagliptin as a potential Resistance Modulator
abstract: E. faecalis is an important opportunistic pathogen increasingly associated with multi-drug resistance infections, particularly through the spreading of resistance genes such as vanA and bla. In the present work, we examined the frequency of two resistance genes in E. faecalis isolated from clinical specimens in Al-Muthanna, Iraq, and investigated the potential of sitagliptin as a resistance-modulating agent. Among 350 samples, 83 isolates (23.71%) were identified as E. faecalis, and they were significantly implicated in cases of urinary catheter and pyelonephritis (p = 0.045). The resistance profile showed maximum resistance to amoxicillin/clavulanate (95.2%), followed by vancomycin (13.3%) and sitagliptin (2.4%). Molecular analysis confirmed the presence of the vanA and blaresistance genes. Sequence analysis of selected isolates revealed single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in vanA (G521A and C560T) and in bla(G244A), leading to amino acid substitutions. Gene expression analysis by qRT-PCR showed that vanA expression was up-regulated by vancomycin (1.47-fold), while sitagliptin exposure resulted in altered expression levels (3.66-fold). Likewise, blaexpression was down-regulated from 1.95-fold under antibiotic induction to 0.75-fold following sitagliptin treatment. A synergistic effect was observed in checkerboard assays when sitagliptin was combined with amoxicillin. Phylogenetic analysis of 16 S rRNA sequences supported the close genetic relatedness of the local E. faecalis isolates with strains reported from China, Hungary, and Tunisia, suggesting possible international dissemination patterns. In conclusion, sitagliptin demonstrated a modulatory effect on the major resistance genes (vanA and bla) in E. faecalis without clear bactericidal activity, indicating its potential role as a resistance-modifying agent. These findings encourage further investigation of sitagliptin as a possible adjunct therapeutic option against multidrug-resistant enterococcal infections.

title: Assessing microbial resistance to Artocarpus heterophyllus leaf-mediated AgNO3 colloidal aggregates using adaptive laboratory evolution
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance poses a major global health challenge, highlighting the need for alternative antimicrobial strategies. In this study, silver-containing colloidal aggregates were synthesized using an extract from Artocarpus heterophyllus leaves and evaluated for their antimicrobial activity and effects on microbial survival under adaptive conditions. Silver-containing colloidal aggregates were characterized for size, structure, and stability, followed by antimicrobial assessment using Minimum Inhibitory Concentration (MIC) and Minimum Bactericidal/Fungicidal Concentration (MBC/MFC) assays. The synthesized silver-containing colloidal aggregates exhibited an average size of 444.00 ± 32.84 nm, a polydispersity index of 0.81 ± 0.16, and a zeta potential of -24.28 ± 10.66 mV. Functional group analysis indicated that phytochemicals mediated the reduction of Ag⁺ ions. Antimicrobial activity was observed against Escherichia coli, Staphylococcus aureus, and Candida albicans, with MIC values of 80, 640, and 320 mg l-1, respectively, and MBC/MFC values of 1280 mg l-1 (E. coli and C. albicans) and 5120 mg l-1 (S. aureus). Adaptive laboratory evolution (ALE) experiments under gradually increasing silver-containing colloidal particle concentrations showed a progressive decline in microbial growth, with no detectable survival at higher exposure levels. These findings suggest that silver-containing colloidal aggregates exhibit antimicrobial activity and may limit short-term microbial adaptation under the tested conditions.

title: Microbial communities on station and train surfaces in Chennai Metro: insights into urban transit microbiome
abstract: Urban public transport systems, particularly metro networks, serve as key hubs for microbial transmission, yet the urban microbiome in densely populated regions like India remains poorly characterized. Understanding these environments is crucial for public health, especially in light of the COVID-19 pandemic and growing concerns about antimicrobial resistance (AMR). This study is the first of its kind to investigate the microbial communities and the presence of AMR genes in the Chennai Metro system. We collected 96 surface swabs from 12 metro stations across two lines, focusing on surfaces that people frequently touch, such as handrails, kiosks, banisters, and ticket counters. Of the collected samples, 47 met quality control standards and were subjected to shotgun metagenomic sequencing, and 41 samples with more than 1 million reads were included in our analysis. Our findings indicate that surface type significantly influences microbial community structure, with kiosks exhibiting the highest microbial diversity. Comparative analysis with global urban data sets revealed unique microbial patterns specific to Chennai, including nine species that were notably more prevalent in our samples than in other urban transit systems worldwide. Furthermore, through pangenome analysis, we generated high-quality metagenome-assembled genomes that elucidated the adaptive strategies of dominant microbial species in this urban environment. Despite their relatively low abundance, several AMR families were widely distributed across the data set, with over 80% of samples containing at least one associated AMR gene, including families linked to rifamycins, multidrug resistance, and sulfonamides. This study lays a foundation for understanding the urban microbiome in India, emphasizing distinct regional characteristics and underscoring the need for sustained monitoring to mitigate disease transmission risks in high-density transit settings. Densely populated urban transit systems are critical hubs for microbial exchange, yet the mass transit microbiomes of Indian cities remain largely uncharacterized, representing a significant gap in global surveillance. Our study provides the first comprehensive metagenomic analysis of the Chennai Metro, a high-traffic transit network serving millions. Our findings highlight the unique environmental drivers shaping urban microbiota in India. Chennai, with over 12 million residents and a metro system serving over 105 million passengers annually, is an ideal yet uncharacterized environment for studying microbial dynamics, surface-microbe interactions, and environmental antimicrobial resistance reservoirs.

title: Draft genome sequences of Bibersteinia trehalosi isolates from western Canadian feedlot cattle
abstract: The genomes of 61isolates recovered from respiratory samples of feedlot cattle (Alberta, Canada) were sequenced (Illumina MiSeq). Draft genomes contained genes encoding resistance to up to seven antimicrobial classes relevant to the North American feedlot cattle industry, with integrative and conjugative elements (ICE) associated with resistance genes.

title: Detection characteristics and antimicrobial resistance profiles of Salmonella spp. isolated from fecal cultures of inpatients at a maternal and child healthcare hospital in Shenzhen: a 5-year retrospective study
abstract: spp. remain an important cause of bacterial gastrointestinal infection, but local data from maternal and child healthcare hospitals remain limited. This retrospective study analyzedspp. isolated from fecal cultures of inpatients at Longgang District Maternity and Child Healthcare Hospital of Shenzhen City from 2021 to 2025. Fecal specimens were processed using routine selective culture procedures; isolates were identified with the VITEK 2 Compact system, with VITEK MS confirmation when required, and antimicrobial susceptibility was interpreted according to Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) M100, 35th edition. Annual positivity and non-duplicate isolation rates were compared using Pearson χtests. A total of 106 non-duplicate isolates were recovered, including 98 from pediatric inpatients. Annual positivity and non-duplicate isolation rates differed significantly across the 5-year study period (both< 0.001) and were highest in 2025. Among pediatric cases, children aged 1-3 years accounted for 79.6%, with the 12 to <24-month group accounting for 52.0%. Resistance was high to ampicillin (76.7%), ampicillin/sulbactam (63.3%), trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (46.6%), and ceftriaxone (36.9%). Resistance to ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin was 12.5% and 14.8%, respectively, although intermediate rates were high. Most isolates remained susceptible to piperacillin/tazobactam and carbapenems. These findings show a concentration of laboratory-detectedamong children aged 1-3 years, particularly those aged 12 to <24 months, and substantial resistance to several commonly used agents, supporting continued local surveillance and susceptibility-guided antimicrobial use. spp. remain an important bacterial cause of gastrointestinal infection in children, but local data from maternal and child healthcare hospitals are limited. This 5-year retrospective study describes the detection characteristics and antimicrobial resistance profiles ofspp. isolated from fecal cultures of inpatients in a maternal and child healthcare hospital in Shenzhen, China. The findings show thatisolates were mainly recovered from young pediatric patients and exhibited high resistance to several commonly used antimicrobial agents, including ampicillin, ampicillin/sulbactam, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, and ceftriaxone, while reduced susceptibility to fluoroquinolones was also observed. These results provide institution-specific evidence for empirical treatment decisions, antimicrobial stewardship, and continued surveillance of enteric bacterial pathogens in pediatric and maternal-child healthcare settings.

title: Analysis of bacteriophage diversity in Ganga river ecosystem: insights from metagenome-based sequencing
abstract: Water from the Ganga River and its tributaries is the main freshwater resource in the northern parts of India and has experienced rigorous ecological deterioration because of the continuous discharge of untreated polluted industrial and household effluents, resulting in increased chemical and microbial loads of pollution. Water is an essential requirement for millions of people and supports a complex ecosystem that includes a variety of microbial species. Among them, bacteriophages are essential for controlling bacterial populations and the dynamics of microbial communities. The knowledge of the diversity and functions of bacteriophages is poorly understood in the River Ganges. Using cutting-edge metagenomic techniques, we explore the diversity of viruses, specifically the bacteriophages in the river, offering a real picture of bacteriophage populations and their ecological functions. Metagenomic datasets were produced by high-throughput sequencing and were used to determine bacteriophage sequences, viral genome similarity, and potential functions. Initial findings demonstrated a significant degree of diversity among bacteriophages. The results demonstrated three families of phage (Casjensviridae, Rountreeviridae, and Peduoviridae).The bacteriophages of these families were identified to infect a variety of bacteria. The results offer important insights into the bacteriophage ecology of freshwater ecosystems, highlighting the necessity for deeper investigation into phage-bacterial interactions in aquatic environments. Gaining a deeper understanding of bacteriophage diversity and their roles in the Ganges can aid in developing phage-driven approaches for environmental monitoring and management, especially in tackling issues like pollution, eutrophication, and antibiotic resistance. These metagenomic results present a genomic basis for investigating environmental bacteriophage and viruses in sustainable water quality management and the generation of bacteriophage-based therapeutic interventions.

title: Residential proximity to intensive animal agriculture associates with increased prevalence of antimicrobial resistance in homes
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR), a global public health threat, affects rural communities disproportionately due to their unique regional exposures, including proximity to animal feeding operations (AFOs), a source of AMR genes. We evaluated residential proximity to AFOs and the presence of AMR genes in the home dust resistome, the collection of antimicrobial resistant genes within a microbial community. We conducted metagenomic sequencing of 534 bedroom dust samples to characterize the resistome for a subset of homes of Iowa participants in the US Agricultural Health Study. We examined the association between the presence of AMR genes in dust samples and the total number of AFOs and distance-weighted number of livestock animal units (AUs) within 2, 5, and 10 km of participant homes, using data from the Iowa Department of Natural Resources. Homes that were closer to a greater number of AFOs and AUs had increased odds of the presence of AMR genes in the dust, including genes resistant to multiple classes of antimicrobials. We found that AFOs were positively related to the composition of the indoor home dust resistome, which may serve as a potential environmental reservoir of antimicrobial resistance with implications for the health of household occupants. This study is the first to detect a positive association between the presence of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) genes in the indoor home dust resistome and residential proximity to animal feeding operations (AFOs), a known reservoir and possible source of AMR in rural communities. Our results indicate that both distance and density were important components of AFO-related AMR risk in rural residential environments. Overall, this suggests that environmental exposures can shape the indoor home dust resistome, which may have implications for the health of inhabitants and increase the risk of AMR infections.

title: Driving factors for the distribution of i/eARGs in livestock and poultry manure and related wastewater across China
abstract: Antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs), as emerging pollutants, have become a growing environmental concern owing to their wide distribution, durability, and potential adverse effects on humans, animals and the surrounding environments. Livestock and poultry manure and related wastewater (LPMW), the major reservoir of antibiotics, has higher abundance of extracellular ARGs (eARGs) compared with other environments. This review summarizes the abundance of intracellular ARGs (iARGs) and eARGs in LPMW in China. The absolute abundance of iARGs and eARGs in LPMW were 10-10and 10-10copies/mL or copies/g, respectively, with sul1, sul2, tetQ, tetW, tetG, ermB, ermF, blaand blaas the main detected i/eARGs types. Subsequently, the study summarized the intrinsic molecular and biological properties, extrinsic drivers, and methodological influences that may influence the abundance of i/eARGs. Discrepancies in the absolute abundance of i/eARGs could be due to factors such as genetic location, sample sources, antibiotic residues and manure treatment methods. Besides, the efficiencies of extracellular DNA(eDNA) extraction methods commonly used for LPMW samples were compared and quantitative methods of i/eARGs were evaluated, which could also introduce subjective bias into i/eARGs abundance. Limitations related to the current eDNA extraction methods and quantitative methods, the establishment of the safety thresholds for eARGs, in situ monitoring methods, and the role of phages in the spread of ARGs were discussed as future prospects. This review highlights the importance of environmental risk assessment for i/eARGs, lay theoretical basis for the effective removal of i/eARGs for further researches and provides advice for future governance and regulatory measurement.

title: Unravelling structurally diverse broad-spectrum antimicrobial secondary metabolites isolated from the stem of Tinospora cordifolia
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is one of the most critical global health challenges of the 21st century; there is an urgent need to discover and develop novel antimicrobial agents to strengthen the current therapeutic armamentarium. Subsequently, natural products serve as a reservoir of unique and structurally diverse molecules, which offer promising opportunities for discovering and developing novel therapeutics to combat AMR. In our present study, phytochemical investigation of the stems of Tinospora cordifolia, an Ayurvedic medicinal plant, resulted in the isolation of 28 chemical constituents. Their structures were elucidated by comprehensive spectroscopic analyses, including 1D, 2D NMR, and HRESI-MS. All isolated compounds were then screened for antibacterial potential against a panel of clinically relevant Gram-positive (Staphylococcus aureus) and Gram-negative (Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Escherichia coli) pathogens. Initial screening at 25 μM concentration revealed three active hits (TC-1, TC-2, and TC-6), which were further evaluated by MIC and MBC determination assays. All three compounds exhibited MIC and MBC values in the range of 0.015 μM to 16 μM and 0.015 μM to 32 μM, respectively. Furthermore, cytotoxicity assessment using murine macrophages (RAW 264.7 and J774A.1) revealed good biocompatibility with a satisfactory selectivity index, while hemolysis assays confirmed very minimal erythrocyte toxicity at the tested concentration. Furthermore, in silico ADME/toxicity analysis using SwissADME and pkCSM predicted favourable pharmacokinetics and drug-likeness properties, although structural optimization may further improve their developability. Collectively, these findings underscore the potential of TC-1, TC-2, and TC-6 as valuable candidates for novel antibacterial drug development.

title: Characteristics of multidrug-resistant bacteria infection and analysis of risk factors in diabetic foot complicated with osteomyelitis
abstract: To investigate the pathogen distribution, antimicrobial resistance trends, and associated risk factors in patients with diabetic foot osteomyelitis (DFO). A retrospective analysis was conducted on the clinical data of 102 patients diagnosed with DFO admitted to Bethune International Peace Hospital from January 2004 to December 2024. The study analyzed pathogen distribution, antimicrobial susceptibility patterns, and risk factors for multidrug-resistant organism (MDRO) infection in DFO patients. 1. Of the 102 patients, 71.5% had MDRO infection, while 28.5% had non-MDRO infection. 2. Multivariate analysis identified diabetes duration, wound duration, anemia, and lower extremity ischemia as independent risk factors for MDRO infection in DFO (P = 0.038, 0.026, 0.035, 0.036). 3. A nomogram prediction model for MDRO infection risk was established based on the four independent risk factors, with an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.906. In patients with MDRO-infected DFO, G+ bacteria were predominantly Staphylococcus aureus and Enterococcus faecalis. G-bacteria were mainly Proteus mirabilis, Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Enterobacter cloacae. Diabetes duration, wound duration, anemia, and lower limb ischemia are independent predictors of MDRO infection. The established nomogram provides an effective tool for evaluating the risk of MDRO infection in DFO patients.

title: Source tracking and transmission of antibiotic resistance genes mediated by core microbiota in black soldier fly larvae bioconversion of doxycycline-contaminated hen manure
abstract: Black soldier fly larvae (BSFL) bioconversion of doxycycline-contaminated hen manure raises concerns about antibiotic resistance gene (ARG) transmission. Although core microbiota in gut may participate in ARG dynamics, the relative contributions of microbiota from manure and baseline larval gut to the BSFL gut resistome remain unclear. Using metagenomics, amplicon sequencing, and cultivable bacteria analysis, we found that: (1) Providencia, Klebsiella, Enterococcus, and Escherichia-Shigella dominated the BSFL gut and served as primary ARG hosts; (2) Fecal filtrate intervention drastically altered gut microbiota and ARG profiles, suppressing Klebsiella (by 95.56%) and Escherichia-Shigella (to < 0.5%) while enriching Providencia (3.53 fold increase) and Enterococcus, with increased ARGs such as tet(59) and qnrD1. Long-read metagenomic analysis indicated that viable manure-borne bacteria, rather than cell-free fecal filtrate, delivered structurally intact ARG-MGE units as key carrier of mobile resistance cassettes; (3) Source tracking (FEAST) assigned the majority of ARBs (> 90%) and their ARGs in the BSFL gut to the baseline BSFL gut source, with manure-derived ARBs contributing 4.80%. Culture-based 16S rRNA gene homology provided evidence consistent with possible manure-to-gut transfer of selected Escherichia-Shigella and Enterococcus. The BSFL gut resistome was more strongly associated with the baseline BSFL microbiota than with manure, but manure still represented a detectable source of ARB and ARG introduction. FEAST source assignments should be interpreted as composition-based bioinformatic estimates rather than definitive proof of origin, due to lack of direct functional tracing. These findings have critical implications for assessing the ecological safety of BSFL-based waste valorization.

title: Serotype and Commodity Contributions to Quinolone Resistance Trends Among FSIS NARMS Salmonella Isolates, 2013-2023
abstract: Food-animal surveillance can identify antimicrobial-resistance patterns that may affect foodborne disease risk, but pooled summaries can obscure commodity and serotype drivers. This study analyzed public FSIS NARMS cecal and HACCP/slaughter-sourcerecords accessed through FDA NARMS Now to examine quinolone-resistance trends by calendar period, commodity, and serotype. Records were filtered toisolates with reported growth collected from 2013 to 2023. Calendar periods were defined descriptively as 2013-2016, 2017-2022, and 2023 to bracket major U.S. antimicrobial-stewardship milestones, including completion of GFI #213 implementation in 2017 and implementation of GFI #263 in 2023; these periods were treated as temporal landmarks rather than causal policy exposures. Outcomes were ciprofloxacin non-susceptibility, ciprofloxacin resistance only, and nalidixic acid resistance. Analyses included commodity-stratified percentages with Wilson 95% confidence intervals, serotype contribution summaries, and binomial models with standard errors clustered by year. The dataset included 42,232isolates; 41,608 were tested for ciprofloxacin and 41,606 for nalidixic acid. Overall, ciprofloxacin non-susceptibility increased from 1.96% in 2013-2016 to 17.84% in 2017-2022 and 25.71% in 2023. Nalidixic acid resistance increased from 1.36% to 17.02% and 24.01%, respectively. These increases were concentrated in chickens, where ciprofloxacin non-susceptibility rose from 1.7% to 28.7% and 42.4%.Infantis accounted for 75.0% of all ciprofloxacin non-susceptible isolates, and Infantis plus Enteritidis accounted for 85.6%. After excluding both serotypes, adjusted period odds ratios were substantially attenuated. Findings indicate that quinolone-resistance trends in FSIS NARMS food-animaldata were strongly shaped by chicken-associated serotype composition, supporting serotype-aware surveillance.

title: Nationwide Cross-Sectional Study of the Prevalence and MIC-Based Antimicrobial Resistance of Salmonella spp. in Poultry in Morocco
abstract: spp. are major foodborne pathogens transmitted through contaminated poultry products. The emergence of antibiotic-resistant strains complicates treatment and increases the risk of multidrug-resistant (MDR). In Morocco, data on antimicrobial resistance (AMR) profiles in poultry-associatedremain limited. This study aimed to assess the prevalence and AMR patterns ofspp. isolated from poultry samples collected in Morocco in 2023. A total of 1339 poultry samples (ceca, turkey, and chicken meat) were collected using a representative stratified sampling approach from slaughterhouses, farms, and retail markets across the 10 regional directorates of Morocco. The isolation ofspp. was performed according to ISO 6579-1:2017, and identification was confirmed via matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight (MALDI-TOF) mass spectrometry. Antimicrobial susceptibility to 15 antibiotics was evaluated using Sensititre EUVSEC3 plates. Minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) were interpreted according to epidemiological cutoff values established by the European Committee on Antimicrobial Susceptibility Testing. MDR was defined as resistance to at least one antimicrobial agent in three or more antibiotic classes.spp. were detected in 155 out of the 1339 samples, with an overall prevalence of 11.6% and regional variation. The category-specific prevalence was 13.8% (48/348) for chicken meat, 12.3% (45/367) for turkey meat, and 10.0% (62/624) for cecal samples. Resistance to nalidixic acid (94.2%), ciprofloxacin (92.3%), tetracycline (63.9%), ampicillin (36.8%), trimethoprim (27.7%), chloramphenicol (16.1%), gentamicin (10.3%), cefotaxime (4.5%), amikacin (3.9%), and ceftazidime (0.6%) was detected, whereas resistance to meropenem was not detected. Overall, 69.7% of the isolates were classified as multidrug-resistant and were mainly resistant to quinolones, tetracyclines, and beta-lactams. These findings highlight the need for strengthened antimicrobial stewardship, improved surveillance, and stricter regulation of antibiotic use in poultry production to reduce public health risks.

title: Remote but not pristine anymore: pharmaceutical pollution challenges management of a high-elevation protected ecosystem
abstract: Remote ecosystems are often assumed to be insulated from chemical contamination; however, increasing human visitation may compromise this perception. We evaluated the occurrence, spatial distribution, and ecological implications of pharmaceutical active compounds (PhACs) in soils from the summit of Roraima-tepui, a high-elevation "sky island" in the Guiana Shield subjected to unregulated tourism and lacking sanitation infrastructure. Surface soils from anthropogenically influenced and naturogenic zones were analysed for 98 pharmaceuticals using HPLC-MS/MS, and potential risks were evaluated using environmental risk quotient (RQenv), cumulative and mixture-based approaches, and antimicrobial-resistance-specific thresholds (RQAMR). Eleven pharmaceuticals were detected, including antibiotics, antifungals, analgesics, and psychoactive compounds. Compounds associated with direct human use (e.g., ciprofloxacin, clarithromycin, acetaminophen) were primarily confined to anthropogenic areas, whereas others (notably fleroxacin, thiabendazole, pregabalin, and sulfadimethoxine) occurred more widely, including in naturogenic zones. These patterns suggest that heterogeneous inputs, compound-specific behaviour, intense rainfall, and shallow sandstone soils may interact to redistribute contaminants beyond their initial points of introduction. Ciprofloxacin reached concentrations up to 186 ng g⁻¹ and contributed substantially to cumulative environmental risk estimates. Several compounds exceeded predicted no-effect concentrations, and screening-level cumulative RQenv values indicated elevated potential environmental risk. Antimicrobial resistance assessment suggested pronounced selection potential for ciprofloxacin in tourist-impacted areas, although resistance genes or resistant bacteria were not directly measured. These findings indicate that tourism-related pharmaceutical residues can occur in remote high-elevation protected ecosystems under tourism pressure and highlight the need to integrate emerging contaminants into conservation and visitor management frameworks.

title: Predicting resistance evolution to guide antibiotic development
abstract: Antibiotic resistance has emerged as a major bottleneck in antibiotic development, frequently undermining promising drug candidates and negating years of research and pharmaceutical investment. Despite growing recognition of this issue, discovery pipelines still emphasize potency and target specificity whereas resistance potential is often considered later in the development process. Predicting resistance remains challenging owing to the diversity of genetic mechanisms, species-specific adaptive pathways and potential side effects of resistance on bacterial viability. However, technological advances now enable systematic mapping of resistance evolution, the dissemination of resistance genes and prediction of the clinical impact. To improve early identification of resistance-prone antibiotic candidates, it is crucial to evaluate five key parameters, including de novo resistance evolvability across pathogens, resistance-fitness-virulence trade-offs, resistance stability, cross-resistance potential and health risk of resistance genes. Integrating these factors provides a systematic, resistance-based framework for classifying new antibiotic candidates and guiding compound prioritization and refinement. Utilizing this framework within the antibiotic development pipeline shifts resistance prediction from retrospective observation to a prospective guiding principle in drug design.

title: Antibiotic resistance profiles and associated factors in aquatic ecosystems with contrasting hydrodynamic settings
abstract: Antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) are ubiquitous in aquatic ecosystems, but the ecological risk patterns and associated factors remain unclear across aquatic environments with contrasting hydrodynamic conditions. Using an integrated analytical framework, we explored interactions among antibiotics, microbial communities, mobile genetic elements (MGEs), and ARGs in a dynamic river and a slow-flow wetland. Antibiotics were widely detected in both systems, with generally higher total concentrations in the dynamic river (50.0-148.4 ng/L) than in the slow-flow wetland (2.5-101.7 ng/L). The total abundance of ARGs was also higher and more homogeneous in the dynamic river (49529.4-58542.5 RPKM) compared to the slow-flow wetland (24091.8-53003.0 RPKM), which exhibited greater spatial heterogeneity. Structural equation modeling (SEM) revealed different ARG-associated factor patterns in the two aquatic ecosystems with contrasting hydrodynamic settings. Bacterial communities and MGEs showed stronger associations with ARG variation in the Qiantang River, with standardized total effects (STEs) of 0.953 and 0.442, respectively, whereas antibiotics and MGEs showed stronger associations with ARG variation in the Xixi Wetland, with STEs of 0.816 and 0.747, respectively. Sulfamonomethoxine (SMM) was identified as the antibiotic most strongly associated with ARG variation in the wetland based on random forest analysis (importance score = 46.90%). This study indicates that the Qiantang River and Xixi Wetland exhibited distinct antibiotic resistance profiles and ARG-associated factor patterns, characterized by a host community-associated mode in the river and an antibiotic-associated mode in the wetland, with MGEs associated with ARG variation in both ecosystems.

Hernia, mesh, microbes, and phage promise: Mapping 35 years of evidence through a systematic review
abstract: Prosthetic mesh is the standard of care for hernia repair; however, mesh-related infections remain a significant biological challenge, with pooled data showing significant morbidity, recurrence, and elevated explantation risk. This study summarises microbiological trends documented over three decades of research, characterises the microbial landscape associated with mesh infections, and investigates how various mesh materials are associated with pathogen colonisation. The objectives are to (i) analyse the aetiology and microbial distribution in mesh-associated infections, (ii) assess the frequency of infection-related events, including mesh removal and postoperative complications, across mesh types and surgical approaches, (iii) describe study population characteristics and procedural contexts where infections occurred, (iv) identify temporal patterns in published reports, and (v) evaluate variables associated with infection-related outcomes as reported in the literature. Following PRISMA guidelines, systematic searches (1990-2025) yielded 4000 records; 584 studies met inclusion criteria, and 32 were eligible for meta-analysis, with uniform groupings by mesh type (polypropylene, biologic, composite, biosynthetic) and period (1990-2007, 2008-2025). Analytical outcomes included incisional hernia rates, surgical site infections (SSIs), explantations, and relevant patient factors, using random-effects modelling. Of the 1213 studies screened, 584 met the inclusion criteria, and 32 were included in the meta-analysis. Mesh use did not correlate with a consistent reduction of surgical site infections (HR: 0.90; p = 0.396). Mesh explantation was significantly correlated with chronic infections (HR: 6.11; p < 0.0001). Polypropylene meshes are most commonly associated with polymicrobial infections, mostly caused by S. aureus, E. coli, and P. aeruginosa. This trend may be a reporting bias, as polypropylene meshes are the most commonly used meshes worldwide. No clinical studies were found for phage-coated meshes. Preclinical evidence demonstrates the strong antimicrobial potential of phage therapy on mesh materials, but clinical efficacy has not been studied yet. The review summarises over 3 decades of hernia mesh research covering the use of mesh composition and materials, associated complications and infection management. With the rise of antibiotic resistance, bacteriophages are becoming a promising alternative for the treatment of mesh infections.

title: Associations of Urinary Triclosan Concentrations Across Gestation and Childhood with the Adolescent Gut Microbiome
abstract: Research on the influence of repeated exposure to antimicrobial chemicals, such as triclosan, on the microbiome is lacking. The goal of this study was to elucidate the associations of time-varying urinary triclosan concentrations with the adolescent gut microbiome. We used data from a prospective cohort based in Cincinnati, OH (enrolled 2003-2006, n = 146), to assess the time-varying associations of urinary triclosan concentrations with adolescent (age ∼ 12 years) gut microbiome diversity and composition. Individuals ≥ 18-years-old were recruited during the second trimester of pregnancy, and urinary triclosan concentrations were measured in pregnant women up to 2 times in pregnancy and up to 7 times in the child from ages 1 through 12 years. At age ∼ 12 years, fecal microbiome diversity and composition was characterized with metagenomic sequencing. We estimated differences in the relative abundance of prevalent (≥50%) bacterial species and gene pathways using linear regression and generalized estimating equations to assess windows of heightened susceptibility adjusted for sociodemographic characteristics. Additionally, we examined sex-specific associations by including an interaction term. The adolescent median Shannon diversity was 3.5 (IQR: 3.3, 3.5). Higher gestational triclosan concentrations with lower gut microbiome diversity [β = -0.13 per 10-fold increase (95%CI: -0.24, -0.02)]. Triclosan concentrations were also positively associated with higher abundance of antibiotic resistance genes and differential abundance of some bacterial species, with the strongest associations observed in early life and at age 12 years. We also found differences depending on sex, with more significant associations observed among males. Our findings provide insight into windows of triclosan exposure that are relevant to gut microbiome composition and the impacts of antimicrobial agents.

title: Design, Synthesis, and Microbiological Evaluation of Differently Decorated Pyrazoles Able to Overcome Antimicrobial Resistance and Biofilm Formation
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance is an urgent global public health threat, killing at least 1.27 million people worldwide and associated with nearly 5 million deaths. Antibiotic resistance has been recently recognized by the WHO as a global health emergency. In this scenario, the research and development of novel derivatives specifically active against resistant pathogens became an urgent need. Pyrazole-based compounds have recently attracted significant interest for their potential antimicrobial activity, particularly against resistant Gram-positive strains such as methicillin-resistant(MRSA). Based on this evidence, we carried out an in-depth investigation of this chemical class by the synthesis of unreported compounds differently decorated on the pyrazole scaffold. The newly prepared derivatives were tested on a large panel of Gram-negative and Gram-positive strains. Interestingly, pyrazolyl ureas (PUs)andshowed excellent minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) values (8-16 μg/mL) against differentstrains and were therefore further evaluated by minimum bactericidal concentration (MBC) determination and time-kill assays and for their ability to inhibit biofilm formation on several MRSA strains. Pyrazolewas shown to exert such inhibition at MIC and sub-MIC concentrations (1/2 MIC and 1/4 MIC), highlighting the pharmaceutical potential of this class of compounds against resistant MRSA. Finally, selected PUs did not affect GM-6114 cell viability, thus indicating the lack of cytotoxicity on healthy fibroblasts, and were predicted to possess favorable physicochemical, pharmacokinetic, and drug-likeness profiles.

title: Integrated In silico and In Vitro Evaluation of Piperine Derivatives as Potential Efflux Pump Inhibitors in Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus
abstract: The increasing prevalence of antibiotic resistance mediated by efflux pump activity represents a major challenge in the treatment of infections caused by methicillin-resistant(MRSA). Efflux pumps such as NorA and MepA reduce intracellular antibiotic accumulation and contribute significantly to decreased antibiotic efficacy. In this study, PBSA-7, a piperine-derived compound, was evaluated as a potential efflux pump inhibitor using an integratedandapproach. Computational analysis, including molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulations, Lipinski rule assessment, and ADMET prediction, was performed to investigate the interaction profiles and drug-likeness of the compound. PBSA-7 demonstrated favorable binding affinities toward NorA (-9.3 kcal/mol) and MepA (-9.0 kcal/mol), with stable interaction patterns observed during the molecular dynamics simulations. ADMET predictions suggested generally acceptable pharmacokinetic properties, although relatively high lipophilicity may require further structural optimization. Functional evaluation was performed by using checkerboard combination assays and ethidium bromide accumulation experiments. In the checkerboard assay, PBSA-7 reduced bacterial growth when combined with ciprofloxacin compared to the antibiotic alone, suggesting that the compound may enhance the antibacterial activity of ciprofloxacin against MRSA under the tested conditions. Ethidium bromide accumulation assays showed increased intracellular fluorescence, indicating potential interference with bacterial efflux pump activity. Taken together, these findings suggest that PBSA-7 may act as a potential efflux pump inhibitor associated with NorA- and MepA-mediated resistance mechanisms in MRSA, highlighting its possible role as an antibiotic adjuvant. However, further experimental studies are required to confirm the underlying mechanism and evaluate its therapeutic potential.

title: Epidemiology, clinical, phenotypic and genotypic characteristics of multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii from Qatar
abstract: In healthcare, multidrug-resistant (MDR) Acinetobacter baumannii is associated with significant morbidity, mortality and limited treatment options. This study evaluates the epidemiology, clinical, phenotypic, and genotypic characteristics of MDR Acinetobacter baumannii from Qatar. We conducted a prospective study from 2017 to 2020 of all clinical Acinetobacter baumannii isolates subjected to phenotypic testing. We performed identification and antimicrobial susceptibility testing using MALDI-TOF MS (Billerica, MA, USA) and BD PhoenixTM (BD Diagnostics, Durham, NC, USA), as well as the E test (Liofilchem®, Roseto degli Abruzzi, Italy). We performed whole-genome sequencing and bioinformatics analyses on bacterial isolates. Out of 536 Acinetobacter baumannii isolates, 62 (11.6%) were MDR, with a decreasing trend. Isolation sites were urinary (42%), respiratory (29%), bloodstream (16%), and skin and soft tissues (13%). Hospital acquisition was recorded in 97% of cases, isolated from older patients with multiple comorbidities and prior antimicrobial exposure, leading to a 30-day mortality of 16%. Phenotypic evaluation revealed extensive antimicrobial resistance to meropenem, ampicillin-sulbactam, ceftazidime-avibactam, ceftolozane-tazobactam, meropenem-vaborbactam and imipenem- relebactam, while the most active agents were tigecycline and cefiderocol. Genomic analysis of 39 isolates revealed predominance of sequence type 2 (n = 27). All resistant Acinetobacter isolates carried AmpC beta-lactamases and the blaOXAAb, (blaOXA-51-like family) family of carbapenem resistance genes. The predominant carbapenemases were blaOXA-23, while 7 isolates carried blaNDM-. Multidrug-resistant A. baumannii was infrequently isolated, predominantly ST2, mainly from elderly patients with multiple risk factors. Extensive resistance profiles limit treatment options, with promising in vitro results for tigecycline and cefiderocol.

title: Intergeneric mobilization of a genomic island mediated by a helper integrative conjugative element from Streptococcus suis to Enterococcus faecalis
abstract: Mobile genetic elements drive antimicrobial-resistance dissemination in Gram-positive pathogens. In Streptococcus suis we previously identified a genomic island, GISsuJHJ17_rpsI, integrated at the conserved rpsI locus and carrying erm(B) and aadE. Here we investigated the genetic features and helper functions associated with mobilization of this island, including its transfer from S. suis to E. faecalis. Genetic annotation established that GISsuJHJ17_rpsI lacks a self-encoded conjugation apparatus but harbours an origin of transfer (oriT) sharing ∼85% nucleotide identity with the co-resident integrative and conjugative element (ICE). We performed filter-mating assays to test ICE-mediated mobilization in trans, constructed precise deletions of oriTGISsuJHJ17 and of the ICE relaxase, carried out complementation, and assessed fitness by growth and head-to-head competition of transconjugants. Filter-mating assays showed that mobilization of GISsuJHJ17_rpsI in the S. suis recipient model required the helper-ICE relaxase and the candidate GI oriT region. Deletion of either determinant yielded no verified transconjugants under the assay conditions, whereas relaxase complementation and chromosomal oriT repair restored detectable transfer. These findings support a model in which the helper ICE provides the DNA-processing function required for GI mobilization, using the co-resident ICE transfer apparatus, as inferred from the ICE gene content. Fitness assays revealed no measurable growth defect or competitive disadvantage associated with acquisition of GISsuJHJ17_rpsI, indicating a minimal short-term fitness cost. These findings show that GISsuJHJ17_rpsI can transfer from S. suis to E. faecalis and integrate at an rpsI-associated site. In the S. suis recipient model, mobilization required the helper-ICE relaxase and the GISsuJHJ17_rpsI oriT region, supporting a helper-ICE-dependent mechanism for genomic-island mobilization.

First report of PLS(A) resistance gene sal(B) in multidrug-resistant foodborne Mammaliicoccus lentus: Molecular characterization and food safety implications
abstract: The emergence and dissemination of antimicrobial resistance through the food chain pose a significant threat to food safety and public health. Our nationwide surveillance of retail foods in China revealed alarmingly high resistance rates among foodborne Staphylococcus isolates, particularly to antibiotics targeting the 50S ribosomal subunit. Among these, Mammaliicoccus lentus (formerly Staphylococcus lentus) is a coagulase-negative species commonly found in food-producing animals and retail foods, increasingly recognized as a reservoir of antimicrobial resistance genes. To elucidate the genetic basis of this severe phenotype, we identified M. lentus strain M177 from retail potato flour exhibiting exceptionally high resistance to tiamulin, clindamycin, and lincomycin, a profile unexplained by known resistance genes. Targeted BLASTp analysis identified a putative ARE ABC-F gene sharing 98.71% amino acid identity with Sal(B), which we designated sal(B). Functional validation confirmed that Sal(B) confers specific resistance to PLS(pleuromutilins-lincosamides-streptogramin A) antibiotics, with tiamulin MIC increased by 128-fold, and clindamycin and lincomycin by 8-fold. Systematic alanine-scanning mutagenesis identified the Loop region as the primary effector of resistance, with Tyr251 playing a predominant role, while Ser262, Pro263, Gly266, Arg275, and Phe276 contributed to varying degrees. Structural analysis revealed an allosteric protection mechanism in which resistance-altering mutations disrupt specific interactions with 23S rRNA nucleotides within the peptidyl transferase center, rather than directly displacing antibiotics. ATP hydrolysis was strictly required for Sal(B) function. Genetic environment analysis indicated that sal(B) is chromosomal and likely intrinsic to M. lentus, with limited horizontal transfer potential. Notably, sal(B) or highly similar homologs were detected in geographically distinct food sources, suggesting a potential distribution that warrants further systematic surveillance. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first report of sal(B) in a foodborne M. lentus isolate, establishing Sal(B) as a mechanochemical allosteric regulator of PLSresistance. These findings highlight the need for enhanced surveillance of ARE ABC-F genes in foodborne coagulase-negative staphylococci beyond the traditional focus on S. aureus, due to the potential threat these resistance determinants pose to food safety and public health.
